subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Bias Blind Spot
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Bias Blind Spot.

hook.text: You think you're less biased than average. That belief? It's itself a bias. Welcome to the blind spot.

buildup.text: The bias blind spot: seeing bias in others while believing yourself to be objective and rational.

discovery.text: Emily Pronin showed that people spot biases in others instantly but deny the same biases in themselves.

twist.text: Knowing about biases doesn't reduce them. People who score high on bias knowledge still show the blind spot.

climax.text: The fix isn't awareness alone—it's processes that check decisions regardless of how objective you feel.

punchline.text: Thinking you're unbiased is the biggest bias of all.

quiz.question: What is the bias blind spot?
options: Seeing bias in others but not in yourself
Being aware of all your biases

details.summary: People readily recognize cognitive biases in others but believe they themselves are relatively objective. This bias blind spot means that learning about biases does not automatically reduce them.
details.whyItMatters: The bias blind spot explains why bias training alone often fails to change behavior. If you believe you are unbiased, you will not take the corrective steps needed to counteract your biases.
takeaways: People see biases in others but not in themselves
Knowledge of biases does not automatically reduce them
Believing you are objective makes you more vulnerable to bias

faq.question: Why does knowing about biases not automatically fix them?
faq.answer: Biases operate largely below conscious awareness through fast, automatic processing. Knowing about a bias engages slow, deliberate thinking, which must be actively deployed. Without systems, checklists, or habits that force corrective steps, automatic biased thinking prevails.

faq.question: What is the most effective way to address your own biases?
faq.answer: Use external systems rather than relying on self-awareness. Structured decision processes, diverse teams, devil's advocates, blind evaluations, and checklists reduce bias more reliably than individual willpower. Assume you are biased and design environments that correct for it.
